_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V: Asfandiyar's Simurgh stage; the duel with Rustam and death. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.zh: 阿斯凡迪亞爾誅西摩爾格

region.zh: 西摩爾格之山（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Seven Stages sec. 6

summary.en: Gurgsar warns of a bird imperious, one like a flying mountain, called Simurgh by merchants: with its claws it beareth off the elephant at sight, the pard on land, the crocodile from water; upon its mountain-home it hath two young, and when it flieth the earth is impotent, the sun is put to shame. The hero laughs — I will sew up its shoulders with mine arrows — and drives at the peak: the Simurgh, swooping down like some dark cloud obscuring sun and moon, essayed to seize the chariot with its talons, but transfixed its legs and pinions with the swords; it beat awhile with claws and beak while strength remained, and then was still. Its young flew off with screams and weeping tears of blood, and Asfandiyar hewed to pieces with his sword that bird now mastered, once so masterful.
summary.zh: 古爾格薩爾又報：「有一飛山般的神鳥——商人稱之西摩爾格；一爪便能擄象、擒豹、拔鱷；山巢之中還有兩隻雛鳥；其翔時大地失色、太陽蒙羞。」王子大笑：「我以神箭縫其羽翼！」驅車至山巔；神鳥如蔽日黑雲俯衝欲攫戰車，卻被劍陣刺穿腿與翼；掙扎片刻便寂然不動。雛鳥泣血哀鳴而去；王子出匣揮劍，將這不可一世的巨鳥碎屍於地。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; pairs with Rustam's Simurgh fosterage (zal-simurgh). No living community restriction.

passages.text: He answered: O Elephant of war in battle-time! Upon this stage thou hast a harder task: be more than ever cautious and alert, thou wilt behold a mount, with head in air, and thereupon a bird imperious, one like a flying mountain, combative, and called Simurgh by merchants. With its claws it beareth off the elephant at sight, the pard on land, the crocodile from water, and feeleth not the effort. Upon its mountain-home it hath two young, and when it flieth the earth is impotent, the sun is put to shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hero laughed: a wonder! I will sew up its shoulders with mine arrows, cleave its breast with Indian scimitar, and bring its head from height to dust. He spying in air a peak stayed in its shadow break and steed, absorbed in contemplation. The Simurgh marked from the mount the box, the troops behind it, and all their trumpeting, and, swooping down like some dark cloud obscuring sun and moon, essayed to seize the chariot with its talons, as leopard seizeth quarry, but transfixed its legs and pinions with the swords, and all its might and glory passed away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: It beat awhile with claws and beak while strength remained, and then was still. On seeing this its young flew off with screams and weeping tears of blood down from the eyry, blurring every eye beneath their shade. When the Simurgh thus sank with all its wounds and bathed steeds, box, and break in blood, Asfandiyar, all armed and shouting, emerged and hewed to pieces with his sword that bird now mastered, once so masterful; then prayed thus to the Maker who had given such mastery to him in good and ill: O righteous Judge! Thou hast bestowed upon me wisdom, puissance, and prowess, hast driven out the sorcerers and been my Guide to every good.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Seven Stages sec. 6 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Simurgh Draws the Arrows from Rustam
title.zh: 西摩爾格為魯斯塔姆拔箭

region.zh: 錫斯坦高地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Rustam and Asfandiyar secs. 23-25

summary.en: Zal, the well-beloved, goes to a lofty height with three censers and burns a plume of the Simurgh; whenas the first watch of the night had passed, gazing from the eminence Zal saw the air filled with the fluttering plumes of the Simurgh. The body of the lion-hearted Rustam hath been bewounded, says Zal; the bird surveyed and sought to heal the wounds, sucked them and, drawing forth eight arrow-heads, stroked with her feathers on the wounded parts, and Rustam was restored to might and Grace. She in like manner having called for Rakhsh employed her beak on him to make him whole, and drew out from his neck six arrow-heads.
summary.zh: 扎勒攜三座香爐登上高地，焚燒西摩爾格的一根羽毛；初更過後，天空中滿是神鳥的翎羽——神鳥臨凡。扎勒泣訴：「獅心之子魯斯塔姆傷重垂危！」神鳥診視傷處，吮淨膿血，拔出八支箭簇，以神羽輕撫傷口——英雄重獲神力與榮光。她又以喙為拉赫什治病，自其頸間取出六支箭簇；駿馬嘶鳴，英雄喜極而笑。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Simurgh's plume is the healing token of the Zal cycle. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When both were set on this bold project Zal, the well-beloved, went to a lofty height, and carried from the palace censers three containing fire. With him went three brave sages. Now when the wizard reached the top he drew forth from brocade a plume of the Simurgh and, having raised a flame within a censer, consumed therein a portion of the feather. Whenas the first watch of the night had passed thou wouldst have said: the face of air is darkened! And gazing from the eminence Zal saw it filled with the fluttering plumes of the Simurgh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just then the bird, surveying from the air and seeing fire ablaze with Zal before it, set seared and sad, swooped down upon the dust. What was't, O king! that made thee need these fumes? said the Simurgh. Zal answered: may the ills that miscreants have brought upon me fall upon my foes. The body of the lion-hearted Rustam hath been bewounded, and my care for him hath fettered me; his injuries raise fears about his life; Asfandiyar hath come against our land and knocketh only upon the door of war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird surveyed and sought to heal the wounds, sucked them and, drawing forth eight arrow-heads, stroked with her feathers on the wounded parts, and Rustam was restored to might and Grace. She said: bind up thy hurts and for a week shun danger, moisten one of these my feathers with milk and stroke therewith inside the wounds. She in like manner having called for Rakhsh employed her beak on him to make him whole, and drew out from his neck six arrow-heads, all that there were. Rakhsh neighed. The crown-bestower laughed for delight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tamarisk Shaft That Blinded Asfandiyar
title.zh: 白楊箭射盲阿斯凡迪亞爾

region.zh: 扎布勒戰場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 27

summary.en: When Rustam knew that humbleness availed not before Asfandiyar he strung his bow and set therein the shaft of tamarisk, the arrow as the Simurgh had bidden, and prayed: thou seest my mind pure in intent; thou knowest that his contention is unjust; so visit not my crime with retribution, O Maker of the moon and Mercury. Asfandiyar perceived him tarrying long from strife: now thou shalt behold the arrows of Gushtasp. Then Rustam quickly fitted to his bow the tamarisk-shaft: he struck Asfandiyar full in the eyes, and all the world grew dark before that chief; the straight-stemmed Cypress bent, intelligence and Grace abandoned him, and the pious prince fell prone.
summary.zh: 魯斯塔姆知卑辭無用，便如神鳥所囑搭上白楊毒箭，向造物主祈禱：「我心純正，其戰不義；願祢勿因我罪降罰。」阿斯凡迪亞爾見他遲遲不戰，喝道：「且看古什塔斯普的神箭！」話音未落，白楊箭已正中雙目——光明之邦頓成黑暗，挺秀如柏的王子彎折倒下，智與恩棄他而去。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the great tragedy of Rustam's career. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Rustam knew that humbleness availed not before Asfandiyar he strung his bow, and set therein the shaft of tamarisk with baneful points, and said: O Lord of sun and moon, who makest knowledge, Grace, and strength to wax! Thou seest my mind pure in intent, my soul, and self control, for much I toil to turn Asfandiyar from strife. Thou knowest that his contention is unjust, and how his traffic with me is all fight and prowess; so visit not my crime with retribution, O Maker of the moon and Mercury!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asfandiyar perceived him tarrying long from strife, and said to him: O famous Rustam! Thy soul is satiate of fight, but now thou shalt behold the arrows of Gushtasp, Luhrasp's own arrow-heads and lion-heart. Then Rustam quickly fitted to his bow the tamarisk-shaft as the Simurgh had bidden; he struck Asfandiyar full in the eyes, and all the world grew dark before that chief; the straight-stemmed Cypress bent, intelligence and Grace abandoned him. The pious prince fell prone, his bow of Chach dropped from his hands; the battlefield was reddened with his blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Said Rustam: thou hast brought this evil seed to fruit! Thou art the man who saidst: my form is brazen, and I dash high heaven to earth. Yet through one arrow hast thou turned from strife, and fallen swooning on thy noble charger. Meanwhile the famous prince had tumbled headlong down from his black steed's back and lay awhile till he recovered consciousness, sat up amid the dust, then seized the arrow by its end and drew it out, drew it out soaked in blood from point to feather.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.zh: 阿斯凡迪亞爾臨終託孤

region.zh: 扎布勒戰場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. V, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 28

summary.en: The son of Zal hath slain me not by prowess, says the dying prince: mark what I have in my hand — a shaft of tamarisk! Not Rustam or Simurgh or bow and arrow have robbed my body of its life in battle, for that hath been the doing of Gushtasp. He said to me: go and burn up Sistan; and now do thou with loving heart receive from me the charge of this my noble son, Bahman, wise, watchful, and my minister; keep him in gladness in Zabulistan, make a great man of him both in deed and word. Rustam lays his right hand on his breast: e'en if I die I will not fail herein, but will set Bahman upon the famous ivory throne.
summary.zh: 垂死的王子道：「殺我的非魯斯塔姆的勇力——看，我手中只握著一支白楊箭！奪去我性命的不是神鳥、弓箭，而是古什塔斯普。他曾命我焚燒錫斯坦……請以愛心接納我那賢明審慎的兒子巴赫曼，養於扎布勒，教他武藝禮樂，使他成為偉人。」魯斯塔姆右手撫胸：「縱我一死，也必不負所託；我將親立巴赫曼於象牙寶座之上。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: In this world have I toiled exceedingly in public and in private to establish the way of God and wisdom as the guide thereto, but when through me the enterprise had grown illustrious, and when the hands of Ahriman were barred from wickedness, fate stretched its lion's claws and brought me down as though an onager! And now my hope is that in Paradise my heart and soul may reap what they have sown. The son of Zal hath slain me not by prowess. Mark what I have in my hand: a shaft of tamarisk! That wood hath closed my lifetime by the practice of the Simurgh and of resourceful Rustam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then thus to Rustam spake Asfandiyar: my time is at an end. Avoid me not, arise and come to me, since all our schemes are changed, that thou mayst hear my last requests upon my son's behalf, my chiefest Pearl. Not Rustam or Simurgh or bow and arrow have robbed my body of its life in battle, for that hath been the doing of Gushtasp. He said to me: go and burn up Sistan; from this time forth I would have no Nimruz.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: And now do thou with loving heart receive from me the charge of this my noble son, Bahman, wise, watchful, and my minister; keep him in gladness in Zabulistan, remembering what evil men may say; instruct him to array the host and order the chase, the combat, and the festival; make a great man of him both in deed and word. The matchless Rustam, hearing, stood and laid his right hand on his breast in acquiescence: e'en if I die I will not fail herein, he said, but bring thy words to pass, will set Bahman upon the famous ivory throne, and crown him with the heart-illuming crown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Rustam and Asfandiyar sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
